paras: The attempted lynching of Maynard Hudson took place early on August 8, 1903, when a mob of more than one hundred white men broke into the jail at Hillsboro, Ohio, to hang Hudson, a young Black man charged with attempting to assault a twelve-year-old white girl. The sheriff had secretly removed Hudson to Chillicothe shortly before, and the mob left after searching the jail, reportedly under orders to renew the hunt. A short dispatch about the attack ran in white papers across the country, several of which warned that a "race war" was feared in the town.

Hudson, described as "a negro" and "a colored prisoner" aged eighteen, was charged with attempting on Thursday night, August 6, to assault Penelope Hindman, a white girl of twelve. He was held in the county jail at Hillsboro, the seat of Highland County. The Hillsboro dispatch also referred to "trouble a few evenings ago between whites and blacks" in the town, without describing it.

The mob, which the dispatch called well organized, reached the jail in the early morning; the Hartford Republican placed the break-in at about two o'clock. According to the Hillsboro report, "the authorities were powerless": policeman Wesley Little was thrown down the high jail steps and badly bruised, while James White was held at the same time under a dozen guns. The men forced their way inside but could not find Hudson, and the Evening World wrote that the leaders "would not believe the negro had been taken away."

Sheriff Elton had taken the prisoner away a short time before. A Chillicothe dispatch the same day reported that the Highland County sheriff had arrived there that morning with Hudson, who would be held for safekeeping because a mob threatened to lynch him at Hillsboro, forty miles away. At Hillsboro the mob disbanded once the jail had been searched, but the reports said its members were "under orders" to renew the search as soon as Hudson could be located.

No later attack on the Chillicothe jail, arrest of mob members, or trial of Hudson appears in the coverage; the last item found, a one-sentence digest in the Anderson Intelligencer on August 19, said only that he "had been spirited away."

The story reached readers mainly as a brief telegraphic dispatch from Hillsboro, printed on August 8 and 9 by papers from New York to Salt Lake City and often paired with the Chillicothe report. Headlines stressed the mob's failure, as in the Evening World's "NEGRO SAVED FROM MOB" and the Topeka State Journal's "PRISONER WAS GONE," or the prospect of racial conflict, as in the New-York Tribune's "RACE RIOT FEARED IN OHIO." The Tribune and some shorter versions emphasized that the mob was white, the Rock Island Argus describing "A mob of 100 white men."

While the dispatch said Hudson was "charged" with an attempted assault, several headlines treated the accusation as proven: the Deseret Evening News called him a "Negro Assaulter" and the Santa Fe New Mexican ran "MOB AFTER NEGRO RAVISHER." Weeklies and digests carried the item for days afterward, from the Hartford Republican in Kentucky, which headed it "Mob Attacks Jail," to the Anderson Intelligencer in South Carolina, which wrote that the attempt to lynch was "for assaulting" the girl. All of the coverage found came from white papers; no account of the attempt was found in the Black press.

A dispatch in the Arizona Republican on August 14, datelined Hillsboro, August 13, gave a different account: about 200 masked men, ready to force the jail with tools, compelled Deputy Sheriff Satterfield to open the door, while Sheriff Elton, warned in advance, had taken Hudson across country to Leesburg. Because it repeats the detail of policeman Little being thrown down the steps, it may be a late, misdated version of the August 8 attack rather than a second one, and the coverage does not settle which. The earlier reports, by contrast, put the mob at more than one hundred and named Chillicothe as Hudson's destination, a point backed by the separate Chillicothe dispatch on his arrival there.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Maynard Hudson
bases: A mob broke into the Hillsboro jail to 'secure and hang' Hudson, who had already been removed, so the episode is an attempted lynching (A2, A9, A1).

A mob of more than 100 tried illegally to take and hang Hudson over an accusation of attempted assault, but he had been removed and was not killed (A2, A8, A9); it is an attempted lynching, not a completed one.

The Hillsboro dispatch (A1, A2, A9) is matched by a separate Chillicothe dispatch reporting the sheriff's arrival with Hudson because a mob threatened to lynch him (A8), and by a later variant account (A20).

accounts.label: Hillsboro wire dispatch (Aug. 8)
accounts.gist: A well-organized mob of more than 100 tried early Aug. 8 to secure and hang Hudson, overpowered the guards, entered the jail and found him gone to Chillicothe; it disbanded under orders to renew the search.

accounts.label: Chillicothe dispatch (Aug. 8)
accounts.gist: The Highland County sheriff arrived at Chillicothe that morning with Hudson, to be held for safekeeping because a mob threatened to lynch him.

accounts.label: Hillsboro dispatch dated Aug. 13
accounts.gist: About 200 masked men forced Deputy Sheriff Satterfield to open the jail; Sheriff Elton, warned beforehand, had taken Hudson across country to Leesburg; policeman Little was thrown down the steps.

framing.detail: Most papers printed the Hillsboro dispatch under headlines on the foiled mob ('NEGRO SAVED FROM MOB', 'PRISONER WAS GONE', 'MOB WAS FOILED').
The New-York Tribune headlined 'RACE RIOT FEARED IN OHIO' and stressed that the mob was 'all white'.
Some headlines presumed guilt ('Negro Assaulter', 'MOB AFTER NEGRO RAVISHER'), and a later digest said the lynching attempt was 'for assaulting' the girl, while the dispatch text said only 'charged'.

conflicts.note: The Aug. 13 dispatch repeats the policeman Little detail, so it may be a misdated version of the Aug. 8 attack rather than a second attack; no other report of a second attack was found.
Unresolved; the larger figure comes from the single later dispatch.
Chillicothe is supported by a separate Chillicothe dispatch reporting his arrival there (A8), the better evidence.
The 19 appears in one condensed reprint and is probably a misprint or OCR error.
